prompt: Match each part of the metaphor to its meaning.

pairs.right: What it would cost to fix now
What it costs every week it is not fixed

right_distractors: What the team was paid for the feature

prompt: Which debt should be paid first, by the lesson?

choices.text: The oldest code
choices.why: Age is not interest.

choices.text: Small principal, high interest
choices.why: Right. A flaky suite wasting hours every day beats a messy module nobody touches.

choices.text: The largest mess in the codebase, whatever it costs to keep
choices.why: Size of the mess is not what decides.

choices.text: Whatever the static analysis tool lists first
choices.why: The tool counts principal, not interest.

prompt: What did Cunningham later say his metaphor had been misread as?

choices.text: A financial instrument for software companies
choices.why: It was always a metaphor.

choices.text: Licence for bad code now
choices.why: Right. Permission to write bad code now and clean up later; he meant code as good as current understanding, changed as understanding grows.

choices.text: A reason to never refactor
choices.why: Refactoring is how the debt is paid.

choices.text: A measure of developer productivity
choices.why: Nothing to do with productivity.

prompt: 'Now we know how we should have done it' falls in which cell of Fowler's quadrant?

choices.text: Prudent and deliberate
choices.why: That is shipping now knowing the cost.

choices.text: Reckless and inadvertent
choices.why: That is 'what's layering?'.

choices.text: Reckless and deliberate
choices.why: That is 'we don't have time for design'.

choices.text: Prudent and inadvertent
choices.why: Right. Unavoidable for any team that learns.

prompt: Which of these are not technical debt, by the lesson? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: No reporting module yet
choices.why: Yes: scope.

choices.text: A booking saved for the wrong day
choices.why: Yes: a defect.

choices.text: A test suite that fails at random every few runs
choices.why: That is debt: it costs time on every change.

choices.text: 'I would have used a different framework'
choices.why: Yes: a preference with no named interest.

prompt: A stable module in an old style has not been changed in three years. When does it become debt?

choices.text: When the team changes its style guide
choices.why: A new guide does not create interest.

choices.text: When a change to it costs far more than it should
choices.why: Right. Until then it charges no interest.

choices.text: Already, because it is old
choices.why: Age alone costs nothing.

choices.text: Never, because it works
choices.why: Working code can still be expensive to change.

prompt: Which test does the lesson give for telling debt from a preference?

choices.text: Is there a nameable interest?
choices.why: Right. If you cannot name a recurring cost, it is not yet debt.

choices.text: Does a tool flag it?
choices.why: Tools count rule violations, not interest.

choices.text: Does a senior developer dislike it?
choices.why: Dislike is a preference.

choices.text: Is it older than two years?
choices.why: Age is not the test.

prompt: Which field of the debt register does the lesson call the one that matters?
hint: Without it, a list of grievances.

choices.text: The name of whoever wrote the code
choices.why: The register names an owner, not a culprit.

choices.text: How it arose
choices.why: Useful context, not what makes it comparable.

choices.text: Where in the code it lives
choices.why: Location helps the fix, not the comparison.

choices.text: Interest
choices.why: Right. It lets each item be weighed against a feature.

prompt: A team decides to keep all clinics in one database until there are fifty. Where does the lesson put that decision?

choices.text: In the sprint retrospective notes only
choices.why: Notes are not kept with the code.

choices.text: In an architecture decision record
choices.why: Right. It records the repayment trigger, fifty clinics, so the debt is paid when due.

choices.text: In the bug tracker as a defect
choices.why: It is not a defect.

choices.text: Nowhere; deliberate debt needs no record
choices.why: Deliberate debt most needs one.

prompt: A static analysis tool ranks an untouched module with a hundred violations above a flaky test suite with none. Why is the ranking misleading?

choices.text: Test code cannot be analysed
choices.why: It can; it simply has no violations here.

choices.text: The tool is broken
choices.why: It works as designed; the design has a blind spot.

choices.text: Violations are not debt at all
choices.why: Some are; the tool cannot weigh them.

choices.text: It counts principal, not interest
choices.why: Right. The suite costs 25 hours a Sprint; the module costs nothing while untouched.

prompt: Five developers each lose half an hour a day over a ten-day Sprint. How many hours a Sprint does the flaky suite cost?
The fix costs 60 hours and saves 25 hours a Sprint. After how many Sprints does it pay for itself?
Automating the deploy costs 40 hours and saves 6 a Sprint. What is the payback, in Sprints? One decimal place.
How does the lesson suggest expressing the interest of a database leaving support?

choices.text: In risk-register terms
choices.why: Right. Probability, impact and the date the probability changes.

choices.text: As hours lost each week, estimated by guessing
choices.why: Its weekly hours are near zero; inventing them misleads.

choices.text: It has no interest until support ends
choices.why: Its interest is the risk it carries meanwhile.

choices.text: As a percentage of the codebase
choices.why: Not a measure of interest.

prompt: Which version of the request does the lesson expect to win?

choices.text: The code is a mess and we need to clean it up
choices.why: It asks for trust and offers nothing.

choices.text: The one with hours and a payback
choices.why: Right. 25 hours a Sprint, 60 to fix, back in under three Sprints: a proposal with a return competes with features.

choices.text: Every professional team refactors
choices.why: An appeal, not a case.

choices.text: We will slow down if you refuse
choices.why: A threat, not a proposal.

prompt: The Product Owner refuses the refactoring this quarter because of a contract date. What does the lesson recommend?

choices.text: Record it, with the interest
choices.why: Right. Record the decision and the interest, and bring it back: a refused debt with its cost recorded is a stronger case next time.

choices.text: Drop the item from the backlog
choices.why: Then the interest disappears from view, not from the code.

choices.text: Do the refactoring anyway, quietly
choices.why: That hides a cost the business chose to accept.

choices.text: Escalate to the sponsor at once
choices.why: A contract date is a legitimate reason; record it first.

prompt: What does the lesson say is the easiest way to get repayment agreed?

choices.text: Tie it to a feature already being asked for
choices.why: Right. Refactoring the payment module as part of online booking.

choices.text: Wait until the code breaks
choices.why: Then it is an incident, not a negotiation.

choices.text: Present a static analysis report
choices.why: It counts principal, not what the business cares about.

choices.text: Ask for a whole Sprint with no features
choices.why: That is the cleanup Sprint, which tends to fail.

prompt: Match each way of paying debt to the debt it suits.

pairs.right: Debt spread thinly through code changed often
A steady stream of medium items
A large debt with its own business case
Replacing a whole system piece by piece

prompt: Why does the cleanup Sprint usually fail, by the lesson?

choices.text: It is too long
choices.why: Length is not the problem given.

choices.text: It treats debt as an event, not a flow
choices.why: Right. It is spent on what annoys, and the habits continue in between.

choices.text: It pays the debt too fast
choices.why: It pays the wrong debt.

choices.text: Product Owners forbid it
choices.why: Often they agree to it; it still fails.

prompt: Why does a big rewrite often reproduce the old system's problems?

choices.text: New code always has more defects
choices.why: Not always; the issue is lost knowledge.

choices.text: It uses the same language
choices.why: Language is not the cause.

choices.text: The same developers write it
choices.why: Same people can do better; the knowledge in the code is what goes.

choices.text: The knowledge embedded in the old code is lost
choices.why: Right. The strangler fig keeps it running while it is replaced.

prompt: A module is scheduled to be replaced next quarter. Should its debt be paid now?

choices.text: Yes, all debt must be paid
choices.why: Not all debt is worth paying.

choices.text: No
choices.why: Right. Every hour spent improving it is lost when it goes.

choices.text: Yes, so the replacement is easier
choices.why: The replacement does not inherit the old code.

choices.text: Only if a tool reports it
choices.why: Tools do not change the arithmetic.

prompt: When does the lesson say a debt is worth paying?
hint: Over the life of the code.

choices.text: When the code is older than the team
choices.why: Age is not interest.

choices.text: When interest outweighs principal
choices.why: Right. Interest over the code's remaining life has to exceed the principal; otherwise the effort buys little.

choices.text: When the Sprint has spare capacity
choices.why: Spare time is not a cost-benefit test.

choices.text: As soon as anybody notices it
choices.why: Noticing is not a reason to pay.

prompt: Shipping booking a week early with a simpler payment integration is in which cell of the quadrant, and what makes it good management?

choices.text: Prudent and inadvertent, so nothing needs writing
choices.why: It was deliberate, and it needs writing.

choices.text: Reckless and deliberate, which is never acceptable
choices.why: Choosing to ship early knowing the cost is prudent.

choices.text: Not debt at all, since it shipped
choices.why: Shipping is when the debt starts.

choices.text: Prudent, deliberate, and written down
choices.why: Right. Recorded with its interest and repayment trigger; unrecorded, the same decision becomes poor management.

prompt: Put the steps of handling a debt in the order the lesson presents them.
hint: Know it, write it, price it, argue it, pay it.
trap: The interest is measured before negotiating: it is the case you bring.

prompt: Leaving the code a little cleaner than you found it is the Boy ___ rule.
